research: https://mayersononanimation.blogspot.com/search/label/Timing?m=0 — characters seem to weigh less in fast motion, and that unreality is what lets physical knockabout be funny; silent comedies were undercranked for this reason. Faster reads as funnier and as less painful, so speed is the safety valve as well as the joke

https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/en/publications/comic-timing-in-contemporary-slapstick-films/ — comic timing in modern slapstick rests on incongruity: an absurd amount of force against a trivial cause (a man being helped into a cab) is the laugh

https://monocle.com/culture/entertainment/the-funny-business-of-comic-timing/ — the gap between a laugh and a wince can be a single frame; a hit that lingers turns into pain, one that snaps and cuts stays comic
https://www.bloopanimation.com/the-art-of-smear-frames/ — (round 1, still holds) a smear gets a limb between poses in one frame; ask a video model for a 'blur' leg and a body that 'streaks'

https://sites.google.com/view/art379/lessons/anticipation-impacts — (round 1, still holds) long wind-up, one or two frames of release, long reaction. Round 1's best take started from a full wind-up, which confirms it: set the wind-up in the still, cock it further
https://veduis.pages.dev/blog/veo-3-video-generation-prompts — for high-energy Veo shots: a sharp subject against motion blur, and literal motion words ('streak', 'blur') over loaded adjectives

https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/ai/20251204-veo3-prompt-writing-guide/ — a mood adjective ('thunderous') can be misread as darkness or a heavy blur; name the physical event (feet leave the ground, body horizontal, springs bottom out) instead
https://www.veed.io/learn/veo-3-1-prompts — describe one primary action with its exact timing; keep the camera locked so the model spends its effort on the action

Round 1 result read as evidence: the penalty still with the foot drawn far back went through first try and gave the cleanest contact (0.8 s, no turn), so all three r2 stagings start from a full, extreme wind-up held in the still, and the motion prompts spend their words on force (feet off the ground, horizontal, airborne) rather than on contact. 'Bends into the car' came from words like 'pat' and 'pops'; r2 removes every gentle verb.
notes: 1) Expect Omni to still take ~0.6-0.8 s from contact to gone. In Premiere: start the clip 2-4 frames before the leg moves, ramp the leg swing and flight to 200-300% so contact-to-gone is 4-6 frames at 24 fps, then drop back to 100% for the car bounce and hold 12-16 frames before the end card. That ramp alone turns 'polite' into 'cannon'. 2) If the lad's feet never leave the ground, cut the frames where he bends in and jump from the contact frame straight to the empty doorway with the car mid-bounce: the jump is the launch. 3) Sell the force in the sound, not the picture: a hard comic 'thwack'/bass punch on the contact frame, a whoosh under the 3-5 frames of flight, a seat-thump plus loud spring creak and a door rattle as the car slams down, then silence. 4) Optional: 2 frames of Directional Blur on the leg at contact, and a 2-4 frame camera shake (Transform position wiggle) on the car slam. 5) CA2-a is attached to every still as the reference for both people, the taxi and the street.

stagings.idea: The penalty, cranked. Round 1's winner rebuilt for force: the figure is caught at the very top of a striker's full-power swing, leaning back, swinging leg wound right up behind him, arms thrown wide. The leg whips through, the lad is lifted clean off his feet and flies flat, horizontal, head-first into the back seat like a human cannonball; the taxi slams down on its springs.

stagings.motion: Locked camera. [00:00-00:01] The figure in the lab coat whips his cocked leg through in a full-power blur; his shoe meets the seat of the young man's jeans and the young man is lifted clean off his feet, flying flat and horizontal, head-first through the open door like a human cannonball, a white streak, gone. Comic cartoon physics, nobody hurt. The taxi slams down hard on its springs. [00:01-00:08] Everything freezes, the figure holding his follow-through, side-on. Thanks.

stagings.idea: The mule. The figure stands side-on facing AWAY from the lad, bent forward with his gloved hands braced on his knees, one leg drawn up and cocked behind him like a mule about to buck. He bucks it straight back without even looking; the lad is launched off his feet into the cab. The not-looking is the joke, and it is more brutal and more cartoon at once.

stagings.motion: Static camera. [00:00-00:01] Without looking, the figure in the lab coat bucks his cocked leg straight back like a mule, a snapping blur; his heel meets the seat of the young man's jeans and the young man is launched off both feet, sailing horizontal and head-first through the open door into the back seat, gone in a flash, legs last. Slapstick cartoon physics, nobody hurt. The taxi bottoms out on its springs with a jolt. [00:01-00:08] The figure stays bent forward, leg still out, side-on, motionless. Thanks.

stagings.idea: The piston. The figure stands side-on in a deep martial-arts chamber, knee hauled up to his chest, foot flexed, body leaning away, coiled like a spring right behind the lad. The heel drives straight out like a piston; the lad goes from standing to gone in one instant, flat out into the cab, and the whole taxi slams sideways on its springs.
